description: Converts syngas (CO + H₂) to liquid FT fuels (jet fuel/diesel) downstream of RWGS or electrochemical CO₂ reduction at 360 kt_CO₂/y reference input. Near-future scenario with CAPEX 100.1 M€ (RWGS route) or 98.8 M€ (ER route).
summary: Fischer-Tropsch synthesis unit converting CO and H₂ to jet fuel/diesel blend, operated downstream of either RWGS or electrochemical CO₂ reduction. Reference scale: 360 kt_CO₂/y upstream input yielding 116.4 kt_FT-fuel/y (RWGS route) or 114.4 kt_FT-fuel/y (ER route), with product LHV 44.3 MJ/kg. Plant lifetime 25 years, 8000 operating hours/year, with ramp-up (30% year 1, 70% year 2), delivery point Basel, Switzerland. CAPEX 100.1 M€ (RWGS route, min 44.9 M€, max 195.8 M€) or 98.8 M€ (ER route, min 44.4 M€, max 193.4 M€) at reference scale, scaling exponent k=0.7, including compressors, heat exchangers, and separation units. Near-future combined CCA 543–1969 €/t_CO₂eq across routes and locations.

description: Fischer-Tropsch synthesis to jet fuel/diesel in long-term scenario; MSP 1150–1750 €/t (RWGS) or 1200–1900 €/t (ER) with 54–92% GHG reduction vs fossil.
summary: Long-term Fischer-Tropsch synthesis with same CAPEX reference as near-future (100.1 M€ RWGS route, 98.8 M€ ER route, k=0.7). MSP 1150–1750 €/t (RWGS) and 1200–1900 €/t (ER) with LT DAC, representing 2.5–3.3× fossil counterpart. Chile achieves lowest MSP (~45% below Netherlands); SOEC reduces MSP by 42–218 €/t in Netherlands but negligibly in Chile. GHG reduction 55–88% (RWGS) and 54–92% (ER) vs fossil. CCA 225–537 €/t_CO₂eq (LT DAC); European Refining Association baseline 500–800 €/t_CO₂eq for e-kerosene. Overall MSPs projected to decline 54.2% from near-future, annual decrease ~5.1% over 15-year horizon.

description: Reverse water-gas shift reactor converting CO₂ + H₂ to CO + H₂O syngas upstream of FT synthesis at 360 kt_CO₂/y reference input, yielding 229.3 kt_CO/y.
summary: RWGS unit generating CO feedstock for Fischer-Tropsch synthesis from CO₂ and H₂. Reference scale: 360 kt_CO₂/y input yielding 229.3 kt_CO/y. CAPEX 28.4 M€ baseline (min 14.4 M€, max 42.5 M€) with scaling exponent k=0.7, including compressors, heat exchangers, and separation units. CO₂ source options: LT DAC (730.0 €/(t_CO₂·y) CAPEX baseline), HT DAC, or PSC (30–70 €/t_CO₂, baseline 50 €/t_CO₂). Near-future PSC-based products ~50% cheaper than LT DAC route. PSC carbon footprint baseline 100 kg_CO₂eq/t_CO₂ captured (range 20–300 kg_CO₂eq/t_CO₂). H₂ sourced from AEC, PEM, or SOEC electrolysis.

description: Reverse water-gas shift in long-term scenario; same CAPEX reference (28.4 M€), enabling FT fuel chain MSP 1150–1750 €/t with 55–88% GHG reduction vs fossil.
summary: Long-term RWGS unit with same CAPEX reference as near-future (28.4 M€ baseline, k=0.7 scaling). Full chain performance via RWGS-FT route: MSP 1150–1750 €/t_FT-fuel (LT DAC, baseline across locations); GHG 55–88% lower than fossil; CCA 225–537 €/t_CO₂eq. PSC vs LT DAC: 7.6% cheaper MSP but 10.9% higher GHG. HT DAC vs LT DAC: MSP 21.5% higher, GHG 1.5× higher. PV-BESS integration (Chile) raises full chain MSP to 1830 €/t (+57.9%); CSP-TES raises to 2245 €/t (+93.7%).

description: Electrochemical reduction of CO₂ to CO as alternative to RWGS for syngas generation upstream of FT synthesis, at 360 kt_CO₂/y reference yielding 225.3 kt_CO/y.
tech_type: Electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO (ER)
summary: Electrochemical CO₂ reduction unit converting CO₂ directly to CO for downstream FT fuel synthesis, alternative to RWGS. Reference scale: 360 kt_CO₂/y input yielding 225.3 kt_CO/y. CAPEX 95.5 M€ baseline (min 68.9 M€, max 122.2 M€) with scaling exponent k=0.7, including compressors, heat exchangers, and separation units. Downstream FT synthesis unit adds 98.8 M€ CAPEX (min 44.4 M€, max 193.4 M€) yielding 114.4 kt_FT-fuel/y. Near-future combined CCA across FT products and locations 543–1969 €/t_CO₂eq. Operating hours: 8000 h/y.

description: Electrochemical CO₂ reduction to CO in long-term scenario; full chain FT fuel MSP 1200–1900 €/t with 54–92% GHG reduction vs fossil.
tech_type: Electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO (ER)
summary: Long-term electrochemical CO₂ reduction enabling FT fuel production. Full chain MSP via ER-FT route: 1200–1900 €/t_FT-fuel (LT DAC, baseline across locations), slightly higher than RWGS route. Life cycle GHG 54–92% lower than fossil counterpart. Long-term CCA 225–537 €/t_CO₂eq. The ER route consistently shows slightly higher MSP than the RWGS route under long-term conditions across all locations and electrolyzer types.

description: Direct CO₂ hydrogenation to methanol at 360 kt_CO₂/y reference input yielding 246.6 kt_methanol/y with CAPEX 120.2 M€ and product LHV 19.9 MJ/kg.
summary: Methanol synthesis via direct CO₂ hydrogenation using H₂ from electrolysis (AEC, PEM, or SOEC). Reference scale: 360 kt_CO₂/y input yielding 246.6 kt_methanol/y, product LHV 19.9 MJ/kg. CAPEX 120.2 M€ baseline (min 59.0 M€, max 181.9 M€) with scaling exponent k=0.7, including compressors, heat exchangers, and separation units. Plant lifetime 25 years, 8000 operating hours/year. CO₂ source: LT DAC, HT DAC, or PSC. Fossil methanol benchmark 261 €/t (2020 average), fossil GHG 1870 kg_CO₂eq/t. Near-future CCA 543–1969 €/t_CO₂eq across locations and electrolyzer types.

description: Direct CO₂ hydrogenation to methanol in long-term scenario; MSP 580–840 €/t with 65–91% GHG reduction vs fossil, lowest MSP among analyzed e-products.
summary: Long-term methanol synthesis via direct CO₂ hydrogenation. MSP 580–840 €/t_methanol (LT DAC, baseline), representing ~2.2–3.0× fossil price baseline; optimistic scenarios potentially <1.5× fossil cost. Life cycle GHG 65–91% lower than fossil. Long-term CCA 225–537 €/t_CO₂eq; European Refining Association baseline 400–650 €/t_CO₂eq. Methanol achieves the lowest absolute MSP among all e-fuel and e-chemical products analyzed in the study.

description: CO₂ methanation via Sabatier reaction (CO₂ + 4H₂ → CH₄ + 2H₂O) at 360 kt_CO₂/y reference yielding 124.6 kt_methane/y, CAPEX 36.8 M€, LHV 49.9 MJ/kg.
summary: Catalytic CO₂ methanation (Sabatier reaction) converting CO₂ and H₂ to synthetic natural gas. Reference scale: 360 kt_CO₂/y input yielding 124.6 kt_methane/y, product LHV 49.8–49.9 MJ/kg. CAPEX 36.8 M€ baseline (min 27.8 M€, max 41.7 M€) with scaling exponent k=0.7, including compressors, heat exchangers, and separation units. Plant lifetime 25 years, 8000 operating hours/year. CO₂ source: LT DAC, HT DAC, or PSC; H₂ from AEC, PEM, or SOEC. SOEC requires high-temperature steam: assuming 90% boiler efficiency, ~1/3 of produced methane (41.6 kt_CH₄/y) must be reused to supply SOEC steam, raising life cycle GHG significantly. Fossil methane benchmark 166 €/t (2020 average), fossil GHG 3984 kg_CO₂eq/t. Near-future CCA 543–1969 €/t_CO₂eq.

description: CO₂ methanation in long-term scenario; MSP 1050–1730 €/t representing 6.3–8.9× fossil price, highest cost multiple among all analyzed e-products.
summary: Long-term CO₂ methanation producing synthetic methane. MSP 1050–1730 €/t_methane (LT DAC, baseline), representing ~6.3–8.9× fossil price—highest cost multiple among all products analyzed. Life cycle GHG 62–94% lower than fossil. SOEC electrolyzers can result in >2× life cycle GHG vs AEC/PEM due to natural gas combustion for high-temperature steam; SOEC long-term energy requirements assumed same as near-future. Long-term CCA 225–537 €/t_CO₂eq; European Refining Association baseline 400–650 €/t_CO₂eq for e-methane.

description: Catalytic synthesis of dimethyl ether (DME) from CO2 and H2 via methanol intermediate or direct route, producing 186.7 kt_DME/y at a 360 kt_CO2/y reference scale.
tech_type: Dimethyl ether synthesis from CO2 and H2
summary: DME is synthesised from CO2 (sourced from LT DAC, HT DAC, or PSC) and H2 (from AEC, PEM, or SOEC electrolysis) via a methanol intermediate or direct catalytic route. At the reference scale of 360 kt_CO2/y input, the plant produces 186.7 kt_DME/y with a product LHV of 28.8 MJ/kg. Plant lifetime is 25 years with 8000 operating hours per year. Baseline CAPEX is 85.7 M€ (range 53.6–135.7 M€) applying a 0.7 scaling exponent and includes compressors, heat exchangers, and separation units. All costs are expressed in 2020 euros. Near-future CCA is 543–1969 €/t_CO2eq,av. The 2020 fossil DME benchmark price is 356 €/t with fossil GHG of 2304 kg_CO2eq/t. Location materially affects GHG performance: Chile with AEC shows 3.6× higher life cycle GHG than Netherlands.

description: Long-term outlook for green DME synthesis from CO2/H2 with projected MSP of 695–1060 €/t and 77–96% lifecycle GHG reduction versus fossil.
tech_type: Dimethyl ether synthesis from CO2 and H2
summary: Long-term (2050) projections for green DME synthesis from CO2 and H2. The minimum sustainable price (MSP) is 695–1060 €/t_DME, approximately 2.2–3.0× the 2020 fossil benchmark of 356 €/t, with optimistic scenarios potentially falling below 1.5× fossil cost. Life cycle GHG emissions are 77–96% lower than fossil DME, the highest GHG reduction range among all assessed fuel and chemical products. Carbon cost of abatement (CCA) is 225–537 €/t_CO2eq,av, with baseline DME CCA below 230 €/t_CO2eq,av. Common model parameters apply: 25-year plant lifetime, 8000 h/y operating hours, 2020 euro monetary basis.

description: Catalytic green ammonia synthesis via Haber-Bosch using electrolytic H2 and ASU-derived N2, producing 277.4 kt_NH3/y at a 360 kt_CO2/y chain-equivalent reference scale.
tech_type: Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis with electrolytic H2 and integrated ASU
summary: The Haber-Bosch process synthesises ammonia (N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3) using N2 from an integrated air separation unit (ASU) and H2 from AEC, PEM, or SOEC electrolysis. At the reference chain scale of 360 kt_CO2/y equivalent input, the plant produces 277.4 kt_NH3/y. Plant lifetime is 25 years with 8000 operating hours per year. Baseline CAPEX is 132.2 M€ (range 107.9–165.8 M€) explicitly including the ASU, compressors, heat exchangers, and separation units, with a 0.7 CAPEX scaling exponent. All costs are in 2020 euros. Near-future CCA is 203–1087 €/t_CO2eq,av. The 2020 fossil ammonia benchmark is 193 €/t with fossil GHG of 2660 kg_CO2eq/t (ecoinvent 3.9.1 cutoff, RER without RU).

description: Long-term outlook for green Haber-Bosch ammonia with projected MSP of 410–670 €/t and 72–96% lifecycle GHG reduction versus fossil.
tech_type: Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis with electrolytic H2 and integrated ASU
summary: Long-term (2050) projections for green Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis. MSP is 410–670 €/t_NH3, approximately 2.2–3.0× the 2020 fossil benchmark of 193 €/t, with optimistic scenarios below 1.5× fossil cost. In favourable renewable locations such as Chile and Spain, the carbon cost of abatement (CCA) approaches ~100 €/t_CO2eq,av, close to 2023 EU ETS CO2 prices. Life cycle GHG emissions are 72–96% lower than fossil ammonia. Long-term CCA is 110–266 €/t_CO2eq,av, with baseline ammonia CCA below 230 €/t_CO2eq,av. Common model parameters: 25-year plant lifetime, 8000 h/y, 2020 euro basis.

description: Urea synthesis via the Bosch-Meiser process using green NH3 from Haber-Bosch and captured CO2, producing 491.8 kt_urea/y at a 360 kt_CO2/y reference scale.
tech_type: Bosch-Meiser urea synthesis from green NH3 and captured CO2
summary: Urea is synthesised via the Bosch-Meiser process (2NH3 + CO2 → (NH2)2CO + H2O) using NH3 from upstream green Haber-Bosch and CO2 from LT DAC, HT DAC, or PSC. At the reference scale of 360 kt_CO2/y input, the plant produces 491.8 kt_urea/y, the highest output volume of all assessed products. Plant lifetime is 25 years with 8000 operating hours per year. Baseline CAPEX is 50.1 M€ (range 24.6–74.2 M€) using a 0.7 CAPEX scaling exponent, covering compressors, heat exchangers, and separation units. All costs are in 2020 euros. Near-future CCA is 203–1087 €/t_CO2eq,av (grouped with ammonia). The 2020 fossil urea benchmark is 202 €/t with fossil GHG of 1406 kg_CO2eq/t (ecoinvent 3.9.1, cradle-to-gate, RER market).

description: Long-term outlook for green urea synthesis with projected MSP of 360–510 €/t — the lowest MSP of all assessed products — and 68–89% lifecycle GHG reduction versus fossil.
tech_type: Bosch-Meiser urea synthesis from green NH3 and captured CO2
summary: Long-term (2050) projections for green urea synthesis via the Bosch-Meiser process. MSP is 360–510 €/t_urea, the lowest MSP range of all assessed products, approximately 2.2–3.0× the 2020 fossil benchmark of 202 €/t, with optimistic scenarios below 1.5× fossil cost. Life cycle GHG emissions are 68–89% lower than fossil urea. Long-term CCA is 110–266 €/t_CO2eq,av, with baseline urea CCA below 230 €/t_CO2eq,av. Common model parameters: 25-year plant lifetime, 8000 h/y operating hours, 2020 euro monetary basis.

description: Catalytic methanol-to-olefins (MTO) conversion producing light olefins (ethylene/propylene mix) at 93.8 kt_olefins/y reference scale, downstream of methanol synthesis.
summary: Methanol-to-olefins (MTO) is a catalytic process converting methanol into light olefins (ethylene and propylene mix), positioned downstream of a methanol synthesis unit in the CO2-to-chemicals chain. At the reference chain scale of 360 kt_CO2/y upstream input, the plant produces 93.8 kt_olefins/y. The reference unit is 1 metric ton of olefin product mix. Plant lifetime is 25 years with 8000 operating hours per year. Baseline CAPEX is 92.1 M€ (range 77.0–107.1 M€) using a 0.7 CAPEX scaling exponent. All costs are in 2020 euros. Near-future CCA is strongly location-dependent: 986–2561 €/t_CO2eq,av in Iceland/Netherlands vs. 5062–26739 €/t_CO2eq,av in Spain/Chile with SOEC, driven by natural gas use for SOEC steam. The 2020 fossil olefins benchmark is 782 €/t with fossil GHG of 3200 kg_CO2eq/t.

description: Long-term outlook for methanol-to-olefins synthesis with projected MSP of 1515–2240 €/t and 50–87% lifecycle GHG reduction versus fossil.
summary: Long-term (2050) projections for green methanol-to-olefins (MTO) synthesis. MSP is 1515–2240 €/t_olefins, approximately 2.5–3.3× the 2020 fossil benchmark of 782 €/t — the highest fossil price multiple among all assessed products. Under optimistic assumptions costs could fall below 1.5× fossil price. Life cycle GHG emissions are 50–87% lower than fossil olefins, the lowest GHG reduction range among all assessed products. Long-term CCA is 395–1730 €/t_CO2eq,av. Common model parameters: 25-year plant lifetime, 8000 h/y operating hours, 2020 euro monetary basis.

description: Catalytic methanol-to-aromatics (MTA) conversion producing BTX aromatic compounds at 97.2 kt_aromatics/y reference scale, downstream of methanol synthesis.
summary: Methanol-to-aromatics (MTA) is a catalytic process converting methanol into aromatic compounds (BTX product mix: benzene, toluene, xylenes), positioned downstream of a methanol synthesis unit in the CO2-to-chemicals chain. At the reference chain scale of 360 kt_CO2/y upstream input, the plant produces 97.2 kt_aromatics/y. The reference unit is 1 metric ton of aromatics product mix. Plant lifetime is 25 years with 8000 operating hours per year. Baseline CAPEX is 16.4 M€ (range 14.1–18.6 M€), the lowest CAPEX of all assessed synthesis units, using a 0.7 CAPEX scaling exponent. All costs are in 2020 euros. Near-future CCA ranges from 986–2561 €/t_CO2eq,av (Iceland/Netherlands) to 5062–26739 €/t_CO2eq,av (Spain/Chile with SOEC, due to natural gas for SOEC steam). The 2020 fossil aromatics benchmark is 605 €/t with fossil GHG of 3200 kg_CO2eq/t.

description: Long-term outlook for methanol-to-aromatics synthesis with projected MSP of 1360–2050 €/t and 55–87% lifecycle GHG reduction versus fossil.
summary: Long-term (2050) projections for green methanol-to-aromatics (MTA) synthesis. MSP is 1360–2050 €/t_aromatics, approximately 2.2–3.0× the 2020 fossil aromatics benchmark of 605 €/t, with optimistic scenarios below 1.5× fossil cost. Life cycle GHG emissions are 55–87% lower than fossil aromatics. Long-term CCA is 395–1730 €/t_CO2eq,av. Common model parameters: 25-year plant lifetime, 8000 h/y operating hours, 2020 euro monetary basis.

description: Alkaline water electrolysis (AEC) producing hydrogen via electrochemical water splitting at 60–90 °C; MW-scale commercially available near-future 2035 scenario.
summary: Alkaline electrolysis cells (AEC) split water electrochemically at 60–90 °C to produce hydrogen at MW-scale. For the 2035 near-future scenario, baseline system CAPEX is 790.5 €/kW (min 437.8, max 1110.3), stack replacement OPEX is 48.9% of system CAPEX, stack lifetime is 75,532 h, and electric energy consumption is 55.1 kWh_el/kg_H₂. Values are inter/extrapolated to 2035 with no CAPEX scaling applied at reference capacity. AEC shows a slight GHG advantage over PEM electrolysis and achieves the best cost of CO₂ avoidance (CCA) among all electrolyzer technologies.

description: Alkaline water electrolysis (AEC) producing hydrogen via electrochemical water splitting at 60–90 °C; long-term 2050 scenario with reduced CAPEX and improved stack lifetime.
summary: For the 2050 long-term scenario, AEC baseline system CAPEX decreases to 527.2 €/kW (min 306.5, max 774.5), stack replacement OPEX is 48.8% of system CAPEX, stack lifetime improves to 87,500 h, and electric energy consumption is 48.9 kWh_el/kg_H₂. AEC retains its slight GHG advantage over PEM and best CCA position among electrolyzers, with the AEC–PEM CCA gap narrowing long-term. SOEC reduces minimum selling price by 42–218 €/t product in the Netherlands vs. AEC baseline, but only 3–11 €/t in Chile.

description: Proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolysis producing hydrogen via electrochemical water splitting at 60–90 °C; MW-scale commercially available near-future 2035 scenario.
summary: PEM electrolysis cells split water electrochemically at 60–90 °C to produce hydrogen at MW-scale. For the 2035 near-future scenario, baseline system CAPEX is 1047.9 €/kW (min 613.0, max 1225.9), stack replacement OPEX is 42.0% of system CAPEX, stack lifetime is 64,026 h, and electric energy consumption is 57.9 kWh_el/kg_H₂. PEM exhibits a slight GHG disadvantage relative to AEC, and the CCA gap between PEM and AEC is expected to narrow in the long-term scenario.

description: Proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolysis producing hydrogen via electrochemical water splitting at 60–90 °C; long-term 2050 scenario with substantially reduced CAPEX.
summary: For the 2050 long-term scenario, PEM baseline system CAPEX decreases substantially to 473.5 €/kW (min 257.9, max 700.5), stack replacement OPEX is 39.4% of system CAPEX, stack lifetime improves to 85,420 h, and electric energy consumption is 53.1 kWh_el/kg_H₂. PEM retains a slight GHG disadvantage vs. AEC, but the CCA gap between the two technologies narrows in the long-term scenario.

description: Solid oxide electrolysis (SOEC) producing hydrogen via high-temperature electrochemical water splitting at 700–850 °C, requiring both electricity and HT steam; near-future 2035 scenario.
summary: Solid oxide electrolysis cells (SOEC) operate at 700–850 °C, requiring electricity and high-temperature steam to produce hydrogen. For the 2035 near-future scenario, baseline system CAPEX is 1739.5 €/kW (min 593.0, max 2770.0), stack replacement OPEX is 27.0% of system CAPEX, stack lifetime is 30,308 h, and energy consumption is 34.1 kWh_el/kg_H₂ electrical plus 8.3 kWh_th/kg_H₂ thermal. HT heat is supplied by natural gas boilers at all locations except Iceland where geothermal LT heat is available. SOEC can result in more than 2× life-cycle GHG emissions compared to AEC/PEM depending on location due to NG-intensive heat supply.

description: Solid oxide electrolysis (SOEC) producing hydrogen via high-temperature electrochemical water splitting at 700–850 °C; long-term 2050 scenario with reduced CAPEX and extended stack lifetime.
summary: For the 2050 long-term scenario, SOEC baseline system CAPEX decreases to 958.3 €/kW (min 566.5, max 1723.3), stack replacement OPEX is 13.8% of system CAPEX, and stack lifetime improves substantially to 71,991 h. Electric and thermal energy inputs are assumed identical to the 2035 scenario (34.1 kWh_el/kg_H₂ and 8.3 kWh_th/kg_H₂). In a CCU methane case (90% boiler efficiency, 124.6 kt_CH₄/y), approximately one-third (41.6 kt_CH₄) of produced methane must be recycled to mitigate SOEC life-cycle GHG. SOEC reduces minimum selling price by 42–218 €/t product in the Netherlands vs. AEC baseline.

description: Low-temperature direct air capture (LT DAC) using solid amine-functionalized sorbent with temperature-vacuum swing adsorption; near-future 2035 scenario.
summary: LT DAC uses solid amine-functionalized sorbents with temperature-vacuum swing adsorption to capture CO₂ from ambient air. For the 2035 near-future scenario, electricity input is 0.48 MWh_el/t_CO₂, heat input is 2.53 MWh_th/t_CO₂, and sorbent consumption is 7.50 kg/t_CO₂. Baseline CAPEX is 730.0 €/(t_CO₂·y) at a reference capacity of 360 kt_CO₂/y with no scaling applied. Sorbent cost of 21.5 €/kg accounts for approximately 20% of product MSP. Location CAPEX factors range from 1.00 (Iceland, reference) to 1.69 (Spain). Near-future MSPs are approximately 50% higher than long-term projections.

description: Low-temperature direct air capture (LT DAC) using solid amine-functionalized sorbent with temperature-vacuum swing adsorption; long-term 2050 scenario with substantially reduced CAPEX and improved sorbent performance.
summary: For the 2050 long-term scenario, LT DAC electricity input decreases to 0.38 MWh_el/t_CO₂, heat input to 1.50 MWh_th/t_CO₂, and sorbent consumption to 3.00 kg/t_CO₂. Baseline CAPEX is 100.0 €/(t_CO₂·y). Sorbent cost declines to 7.4 €/kg. Compared to LT DAC, post-combustion capture (PSC) offers 7.6% lower average MSP but 10.9% higher GHG, while HT DAC MSP is 21.5% higher with 1.5× the GHG. Sorbent cost and consumption decline accounts for 33.4% of total MSP reduction potential (~405 €/t product). Average MSP declines 54.2% from near- to long-term (5.1% per year over 15 years).

description: High-temperature direct air capture (HT DAC) via aqueous hydroxide absorption with high-temperature calcination for sorbent regeneration; NG-fired boilers supply HT heat; near-future 2035 scenario.
summary: HT DAC employs aqueous hydroxide-based absorption with a high-temperature calcination step for sorbent regeneration, with HT heat supplied by natural gas boilers at all locations. For the 2035 near-future scenario, absolute CAPEX and energy inputs are not individually reported; ambient condition effects on CAPEX and energy are neglected. Compared to LT DAC (long-term, Iceland, AEC basis), HT DAC average MSP is 21.5% higher and life-cycle GHG is 1.5× higher, primarily due to NG-intensive calcination. No location-specific CAPEX or energy correction was applied.

description: High-temperature direct air capture (HT DAC) via aqueous hydroxide absorption with high-temperature calcination; NG-fired boilers at all locations; long-term 2050 scenario.
summary: For the 2050 long-term scenario, HT DAC retains its aqueous hydroxide absorption process with NG-fired boilers providing HT heat for calcination at all locations, with no location-specific CAPEX or energy corrections applied. Absolute cost and energy input values are not individually reported. Compared to LT DAC (long-term, Iceland, AEC basis), HT DAC average MSP is 21.5% higher and life-cycle GHG is 1.5× higher, driven primarily by the NG-intensive calcination step.

description: Post-combustion CO₂ capture from industrial point sources (e.g., cement plants) using amine absorbers, producing 1 tonne of captured CO₂ per unit. Near-future (2035) scenario.
summary: Post-combustion capture (PSC) using amine absorbers is applied to industrial point sources such as cement plants. For 2035, capture cost ranges €30–70/t_CO₂ with a baseline of €50/t_CO₂. The lifecycle carbon footprint baseline is 100 kg_CO₂eq/t_CO₂ captured (range 20–300). PSC products are on average ~50% cheaper than low-temperature DAC (LT DAC) near-future and ~7.6% cheaper long-term, but emit ~10.9% more GHG per tonne of product than LT DAC long-term.

description: Post-combustion CO₂ capture from industrial point sources (e.g., cement plants) using amine absorbers, producing 1 tonne of captured CO₂ per unit. Long-term (2050) scenario.
summary: Post-combustion capture (PSC) using amine absorbers applied to industrial point sources such as cement plants. For 2050, the cost range is unchanged from the near-future scenario at €30–70/t_CO₂ with a baseline of €50/t_CO₂ (no separate long-term value stated). Carbon footprint baseline remains 100 kg_CO₂eq/t_CO₂. PSC is ~7.6% cheaper than LT DAC long-term products (FT fuels RWGS, Iceland, AEC), but emits ~10.9% more GHG per tonne of product than LT DAC long-term.

description: Utility-scale photovoltaic electricity generation in Spain (Tabernas), near-future (2035) scenario. LCOE baseline 34.7 €/MWh_el; GHG baseline 66.0 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_el.
summary: Utility-scale PV in Spain (Tabernas) for 2035 yields an LCOE baseline of 34.7 €/MWh_el (range 23.0–45.0). GHG intensity baseline is 66.0 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_el (range 20.0–123.8). Low-temperature heat supply is sourced from industrial processes or solar thermal collectors. This location serves as a reference for southern European solar conditions and is used in techno-economic comparisons of e-fuel and hydrogen pathways.

description: Photovoltaic system coupled with battery energy storage (PV-BESS) enabling 8000 full-load hours per year, near-future (2035) scenario. LCOE baseline 68.2 €/MWh_el.
tech_type: PV with Battery Energy Storage System (PV-BESS)
summary: PV with Battery Energy Storage System (PV-BESS) is designed to provide 8000 h/y full-load equivalent operation by storing excess solar generation. For 2035, the LCOE baseline is 68.2 €/MWh_el (range 50.0–88.0), approximately double the PV-only cost, reflecting storage capital costs. GHG intensity baseline is 124.3 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_el (range 95.0–153.0), nearly double PV-only due to battery manufacturing footprint. Using PV-BESS instead of PV-only increases minimum selling price (MSP) of downstream products by ~57.9% and CCA by ~4.4×.

description: Utility-scale photovoltaic electricity generation in Spain (Tabernas), long-term (2050) scenario. LCOE baseline 18.1 €/MWh_el; GHG baseline 57.2 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_el.
summary: Utility-scale PV in Spain (Tabernas) for 2050 achieves an LCOE baseline of 18.1 €/MWh_el (range 14.0–20.4), ~48% lower than the 2035 baseline. GHG intensity drops to 57.2 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_el (range 15.9–98.4), a ~41% reduction versus near-future. Long-term Central European electricity is broadly expected below 25–50 €/MWh during most hours March–October. Spain PV products carry ~50% higher life-cycle GHG than offshore wind Netherlands products.

description: Photovoltaic system with battery energy storage (PV-BESS) enabling 8000 full-load hours per year, long-term (2050) scenario. LCOE baseline 45.2 €/MWh_el.
tech_type: PV with Battery Energy Storage System (PV-BESS)
summary: PV-BESS for 2050 achieves an LCOE baseline of 45.2 €/MWh_el (range 30.0–66.0), a ~34% reduction from the 2035 baseline of 68.2 €/MWh_el. GHG intensity for PV-BESS long-term is not stated separately. Compared to CSP-TES (another storage-inclusive option), PV-BESS products carry on average ~2 t_CO₂eq/t_product more GHG. CCA with PV-BESS remains 4.4× higher than without storage in the long-term scenario.

description: Offshore wind electricity generation near Rotterdam (Netherlands), near-future (2035) scenario. LCOE baseline 63.9 €/MWh_el; GHG baseline 12.6 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_el.
summary: Offshore wind in the Netherlands (near Rotterdam) for 2035 yields an LCOE baseline of 63.9 €/MWh_el (range 50.0–80.0) at 8000 full-load hours per year, enabling continuous operation without dedicated storage. GHG intensity baseline is 12.6 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_el (range 4.6–19.0), the lowest life-cycle GHG among European electricity sources in the model. Low-temperature heat is sourced from industrial residual heat. Netherlands electricity represents offshore wind in all modelling.

description: Offshore wind electricity generation near Rotterdam (Netherlands), long-term (2050) scenario. LCOE baseline 40.0 €/MWh_el; GHG baseline 11.3 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_el.
summary: Offshore wind in the Netherlands for 2050 achieves an LCOE baseline of 40.0 €/MWh_el (range 25.0–55.0), a ~37% reduction from 2035. GHG intensity decreases to 11.3 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_el (range 4.4–18.2), a ~9% reduction versus near-future. Netherlands offshore wind products have ~6% lower life-cycle GHG than Iceland geothermal products, ~50% lower than Spain PV, and ~55% lower than Chile PV, making it the lowest GHG electricity source among European locations modelled.

description: Geothermal electricity (and low-temperature heat) generation in Iceland, co-located with the Climeworks Hellisheidi DAC plant, near-future (2035) scenario. LCOE baseline 25.6 €/MWh_el.
summary: Geothermal energy in Iceland (Hellisheidi) for 2035 provides baseload electricity at an LCOE baseline of 25.6 €/MWh_el (range 16.5–35.0) at 8000 h/y full-load, without dedicated storage costs. GHG intensity baseline is 17.0 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_el (range 8.5–32.0). Low-temperature heat (<100 °C) is provided by geothermal, while high-temperature heat (>100 °C) still relies on natural gas boilers. Iceland is the cheapest electricity location near-future (~15% cheaper than Netherlands, ~17% cheaper than Chile, ~29% cheaper than Spain on average) and achieves the lowest CCA near-future across most products.

description: Geothermal electricity and low-temperature heat generation in Iceland (Hellisheidi), long-term (2050) scenario. Electricity cost not separately stated; GHG baseline 13.9 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_el.
summary: Geothermal energy in Iceland for 2050 sees a GHG intensity reduction to a baseline of 13.9 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_el (range 5.8–21.9), a ~63% decrease versus the 2035 baseline of 17.0. No separate long-term electricity cost is stated. Iceland continues to offer the lowest CCA long-term for most e-fuel and hydrogen products. High-temperature heat (>100 °C) is still assumed to require supplementary sources (e.g., natural gas boilers) in the long-term scenario.

description: Concentrated solar power with thermal energy storage (CSP-TES) enabling 8000 full-load hours per year, near-future (2035) scenario. LCOE baseline 82.1 €/MWh_el.
tech_type: Parabolic trough / tower CSP with molten-salt TES
summary: CSP with thermal energy storage (CSP-TES) provides dispatchable solar electricity at 8000 h/y full-load equivalent in Spain (Tabernas) or Chile (Sierra Gorda). For 2035, the LCOE baseline is 82.1 €/MWh_el (range 79.0–88.0), the highest among electricity sources modelled. GHG intensity baseline is 16.0 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_el (range 9.8–24.3), comparable to offshore wind and geothermal. The storage-inclusive LCOE reflects thermal storage capital; long-term GHG for CSP-TES is not separately stated.

description: Concentrated solar power with thermal energy storage (CSP-TES) enabling 8000 full-load hours per year, long-term (2050) scenario. LCOE baseline 63.1 €/MWh_el.
tech_type: Parabolic trough / tower CSP with molten-salt TES
summary: CSP-TES for 2050 achieves an LCOE baseline of 63.1 €/MWh_el (range 47.0–88.0), a ~23% reduction from 2035. GHG intensity for CSP-TES long-term is not separately stated. In downstream product comparisons (Chile, FT fuels via RWGS, AEC, LT DAC), CSP-TES raises MSP of FT fuel (RWGS) to 2245 €/t (+93.7% vs. no-storage baseline) and increases CCA by ~1.5×. CSP-TES GHG is approximately equal to offshore wind Netherlands (~10% higher), while PV-BESS products carry ~2 t_CO₂eq/t_product more than CSP-TES.

description: PV-coupled battery energy storage system (PV-BESS) providing dispatchable electricity at 8000 full-load hours per year; LCOE includes storage costs.
summary: Near-future (2035) PV-BESS system with an LCOE of 68.2 €/MWh_el (range: 50–88 €/MWh_el) and GHG intensity of 124.3 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_el (range: 95–153). Compared to standalone PV, PV-BESS increases downstream CCU product MSP by an average of 51.2%; FT fuels (RWGS) rise by 57.9% to 1830 €/t. Carbon capture avoidance cost (CCA) is 4.4× higher with PV-BESS than without storage. Analysis based on Chile location with AEC electrolysis and LT DAC.

description: PV-coupled battery energy storage system (PV-BESS) long-term scenario with reduced LCOE compared to 2035.
summary: Long-term (2050) PV-BESS scenario with an LCOE of 45.2 €/MWh_el (range: 30–66 €/MWh_el). GHG intensity is not reported for this scenario. Average GHG of PV-BESS is approximately 2 t_CO₂eq/t_product higher than CSP-TES under long-term Chile conditions. Modular assumption applied with no economy-of-scale scaling factor, consistent with WCT and DAC assumptions.

description: Natural gas boiler supplying high-temperature process heat (>100°C) to CCU plants at all modelled locations including Iceland, Netherlands, Spain, and Chile.
summary: Near-future (2035) NG boiler providing HT steam (>100°C) at a cost of 25.0 €/MWh_th (range: 15.0–40.0 €/MWh_th) with an assumed thermal efficiency of 90%. GHG intensity is 232.5 kg_CO₂eq/MWh_th. Required for SOEC electrolyser HT steam supply and HT DAC calcination. SOEC with NG boiler yields >2× lifecycle GHG vs. AEC/PEM depending on location. HT DAC has 21.5% higher MSP and 1.5× higher GHG than LT DAC due to NG-intensive calcination. In the SOEC methane case, ~1/3 of produced CCU methane (41.6 kt_CH₄/y of 124.6 kt_CH₄/y total) must be recycled to offset NG boiler lifecycle GHG.

description: Natural gas boiler for high-temperature process heat (>100°C); long-term scenario with no updated cost or GHG data reported.
summary: Long-term (2050) scenario for NG boiler supplying HT heat (>100°C). No long-term cost or GHG values are reported; only near-future values are available from Table 3. NG boilers remain required for HT processes at all locations including Iceland, which substitutes only LT heat (<100°C) with geothermal energy. Netherlands uses industrial residual heat for LT processes (7.5 €/MWh_th, range 5–10 €/MWh_th); Spain and Chile use industrial processes or solar thermal collectors for LT heat.

description: Wet cooling tower for process heat rejection across all CCU plant configurations and locations; modular assumption with no economy-of-scale scaling.
summary: Near-future (2035) wet cooling tower (WCT) providing heat rejection across all CCU plant locations. Electricity consumption is 33.0 Wh_el/kWh_cooling (range: 5–60 Wh_el/kWh_cooling). CAPEX baseline is 24,500 €/MW_cooling (range: 22,000–27,000 €/MW_cooling). WCT capacity in model ranges from 8.0 to 284.2 MW_cooling. Modular assumption applied with no economy-of-scale scaling factor. No separate OPEX or LCA/GHG values reported for WCT alone.

description: Wet cooling tower for process heat rejection across all CCU plant configurations; long-term scenario using same parameters as near-future baseline.
summary: Long-term (2050) wet cooling tower (WCT) scenario. No separate long-term values are reported; same parameters as the near-future (2035) baseline are applied. Electricity consumption remains 33.0 Wh_el/kWh_cooling (range: 5–60 Wh_el/kWh_cooling) and CAPEX baseline is 24,500 €/MW_cooling (range: 22,000–27,000 €/MW_cooling). WCT capacity range in model: 8.0–284.2 MW_cooling. Modular assumption with no scaling factor applied, consistent with DAC and BESS assumptions.

description: Alkaline water electrolysis operating at 60-90°C with MW-scale commercial deployment and flexible operation capability.
summary: Currently dominant market technology alongside PEM with mature commercial deployment. Operates at 60-90°C with baseline electric efficiency of 55.1 kWh_el/kg_H2 (range 47.5–75.0). System CAPEX 790.5 €/kW with stack replacement at 48.9% of CAPEX. Stack lifetime approximately 75,532 hours.

description: Alkaline water electrolysis long-term future with improved efficiency and reduced capital costs.
summary: Long-term future development showing improved performance. Electric efficiency 48.9 kWh_el/kg_H2 (range 45.47–52.0). System CAPEX reduced to 527.2 €/kW, representing 33% reduction from near-term. Stack replacement 48.8% of CAPEX. Stack lifetime approximately 87,500 hours.

description: Proton exchange membrane electrolysis operating at 60-90°C with MW-scale commercial deployment.
summary: Currently dominant market technology alongside AEC with mature commercial deployment. Operates at 60-90°C with baseline electric efficiency of 57.9 kWh_el/kg_H2 (range 48.8–83.0). System CAPEX 1047.9 €/kW with stack replacement at 42.0% of CAPEX. Stack lifetime approximately 64,026 hours.

description: Proton exchange membrane electrolysis long-term future with improved efficiency and significantly reduced capital costs.
summary: Long-term future development with significant cost reduction. Electric efficiency 53.1 kWh_el/kg_H2 (range 47.0–64.0). System CAPEX reduced to 473.5 €/kW, representing 55% reduction from near-term. Stack replacement 39.4% of CAPEX. Stack lifetime approximately 85,420 hours.

description: Solid oxide electrolysis operating at 700-850°C with high-temperature thermal integration and natural gas heat input. Not yet commercialized at scale.
summary: High-temperature electrochemical process below thermoneutral conditions. Operating temperature 700-850°C. Baseline electric requirement 34.1 kWh_el/kg_H2 (range 26.6–38.1) plus thermal energy 8.3 kWh_th/kg_H2 (range 6.7–11.0). System CAPEX 1739.5 €/kW with stack replacement at 27.0% of CAPEX. Stack lifetime approximately 30,308 hours. High lifecycle GHG emissions from natural gas input for steam generation.

description: Solid oxide electrolysis long-term future with improved stack lifetime and reduced capital costs.
summary: Long-term future development with significantly improved economics. Electric efficiency assumed 34.1 kWh_el/kg_H2 and thermal energy 8.3 kWh_th/kg_H2 (same as near-term). System CAPEX reduced to 958.3 €/kW, representing 45% reduction. Stack replacement 13.8% of CAPEX. Stack lifetime improved to approximately 71,991 hours. Economic advantage of 42-218 €/t in Netherlands but negligible benefits in Chile (3-11 €/t reduction).

description: Low-temperature direct air capture using temperature-vacuum swing adsorption with amine-functionalized sorbent. Energy consumption varies significantly with ambient conditions.
summary: Temperature-vacuum swing adsorption process. Baseline electricity requirement 0.48 MWh_el/t_CO2 (range 0.25–0.70) and heat <100°C at 2.53 MWh_th/t_CO2 (range 1.75–3.30). Sorbent consumption 7.50 kg/t_CO2 (minimum 3.00) at cost 21.5 €/kg_sorbent (range 13.0–30.0). System CAPEX 730.0 €/t_CO2/year. Location-dependent performance factors from 1.00 (Iceland) to 1.69 (Spain) for CAPEX. Reference application: Climeworks Mammoth plant at 36 kt_CO2/year.

description: Low-temperature direct air capture long-term future with significantly improved sorbent efficiency and reduced energy requirements.
summary: Long-term development with improved performance. Baseline electricity requirement 0.38 MWh_el/t_CO2 (range 0.25–0.50) and heat 1.50 MWh_th/t_CO2. Sorbent consumption reduced to 3.00 kg/t_CO2 at significantly lower cost of 7.4 €/kg_sorbent (range 1.8–13.0). System CAPEX reduced to 237.0 €/t_CO2/year. Sorbent cost decline and consumption reduction attributed to 33.4% of total MSP reduction from near to long-term future.

description: High-temperature direct air capture using aqueous absorption process with energy-intensive calcination requiring natural gas.
summary: Aqueous absorption DAC process with natural gas-driven high-temperature calcination. Carbon footprint of CO2 feedstock estimated at 100 kg_CO2eq/t_CO2 (typical range 20–300 depending on absorption process). Minimum selling prices 21.5% higher than low-temperature DAC in near-term due to energy-intensive calcination. No cost advantage over point-source capture in this period. Lower data granularity compared to low-temperature DAC.

description: High-temperature direct air capture long-term future development with potential improvements but without clear cost advantages.
summary: Long-term future outlook shows high-temperature DAC does not offer distinct advantages over low-temperature adsorption DAC despite natural gas utilization. No cost benefits identified compared with LT-DAC in long-term horizon. Technology development constrained by fundamental energy requirements and calcination processes.

description: Postcombustion CO2 capture from industrial flue gas using amine-based absorbents. Typical capture cost of €50/t_CO2 for hard-to-abate industries like cement production.
summary: Point-source capture uses amine-based absorbents to extract CO2 from industrial flue gas with an average capture cost of €50/t_CO2. PSC products average 50% cheaper than LT DAC alternatives in the near term and may emit 10.9% more GHGs. The process serves as a catalyst for technological advancement while DAC capacities remain limited. Carbon footprint of captured CO2 is typically 100 kg_CO2eq/t_CO2.

description: Postcombustion CO2 capture for long-term future scenarios post-2035. Benefits from electricity cost reductions though cost differences versus DAC diminish.
summary: Long-term PSC performance is driven by electricity consumption dominance for downstream electrolysis. Cost advantages versus long-term DAC diminish as relative importance of capture cost decreases. CO2 emissions from fossil-based PSC do not lead to net-zero emissions even if considered climate neutral in regulations.

description: Fischer-Tropsch synthesis via reverse water-gas shift (RWGS) route converting CO2 to FT-fuel with intermediate CO production capacity of 229.3 kt/y and final output of 116.4 kt_FT-fuel/y.
summary: Two-stage Fischer-Tropsch synthesis via RWGS produces CO as intermediate product from 360 kt_CO2/y input. RWGS unit CAPEX is €28.4M baseline (range €14.4–42.5M), FT synthesis CAPEX is €100.1M baseline (range €44.9–195.8M). MSP ranges 1150–1750 €/t_product with cost per ton CO2 avoided of 543–1969 €/t_CO2eq,av. Life cycle GHG emissions are 55–88% lower than fossil diesel counterpart (44.3 MJ/kg LHV, 4164 kg_CO2eq/t).

description: Long-term Fischer-Tropsch via RWGS with MSP 2.5–3.3 times higher than fossil counterpart and improved cost reduction from electrolysis efficiency and sorbent improvements.
summary: Long-term FT synthesis via RWGS maintains MSP of 1150–1750 €/t_product (2.5–3.3 times fossil price). Cost per ton CO2 avoided improves to 225–537 €/t_CO2eq,av baseline range. Major cost reduction drivers include electricity cost reduction (~20% of MSP reduction), electrolyzer efficiency improvements, and sorbent cost/consumption decline (33.4% of total). Location performance shows Chile cheapest at 5% lower than Spain, 15% lower than Iceland, 45% lower than Netherlands. Most optimistic scenario achieves less than 1.5 times fossil price.

description: Direct methanol synthesis from CO2 and hydrogen with production capacity of 246.6 kt_methanol/y from 360 kt_CO2/y input and CAPEX of €120.2M baseline.
summary: Direct-route methanol synthesis from CO2 and hydrogen produces 246.6 kt_methanol/y from 360 kt_CO2/y input. CAPEX baseline €120.2M (range €59.0–181.9M). MSP ranges 580–840 €/t_product with cost per ton CO2 avoided of 543–1969 €/t_CO2eq,av. Life cycle GHG emissions are 65–91% lower than fossil counterpart (19.9 MJ/kg LHV, 1870 kg_CO2eq/t, fossil price 261 €/t).

description: Long-term methanol synthesis with improved economics reaching MSP 2.2–3.0 times fossil price and cost per ton CO2 avoided below 230 €/t_CO2eq,av.
summary: Long-term methanol synthesis maintains production of 246.6 kt_methanol/y with MSP 580–840 €/t_product (2.2–3.0 times fossil price). Cost per ton CO2 avoided improves to 225–537 €/t_CO2eq,av baseline range, estimated to fall below 230 €/t_CO2eq,av. Life cycle GHG emissions remain 65–91% lower than fossil counterpart. Economics align well with existing EU climate change mitigation policies and incentives. European Refining Association estimates long-term cost at 400–650 €/t_CO2eq,av.

description: Methanation synthesis from CO2 and hydrogen producing 124.6 kt_methane/y from 360 kt_CO2/y input with CAPEX of €36.8M baseline.
summary: Methanation synthesizes methane from CO2 and hydrogen, producing 124.6 kt_methane/y from 360 kt_CO2/y input. CAPEX baseline €36.8M (range €27.8–41.7M). MSP ranges 1050–1730 €/t_product with cost per ton CO2 avoided of 543–1969 €/t_CO2eq,av. Life cycle GHG emissions are 62–94% lower than fossil counterpart (49.8 MJ/kg LHV, 3984 kg_CO2eq/t, fossil price 166 €/t). For SOEC operation, 90% methane boiler efficiency would require ~41.6 kt_CH4 reused to reduce life cycle GHG emissions (~1/3 of produced methane).

description: Long-term methanation with MSP 6.3–8.9 times higher than fossil counterpart, representing the highest multiplier among major CO2 conversion products.
summary: Long-term methanation maintains MSP 1050–1730 €/t_product (6.3–8.9 times fossil price). Cost per ton CO2 avoided improves to 225–537 €/t_CO2eq,av baseline range. Life cycle GHG emissions remain 62–94% lower than fossil counterpart. Methanation faces the highest cost challenge relative to fossil counterpart among major products examined due to its high energy requirements.

description: Dimethyl ether synthesis from CO2 and hydrogen producing 186.7 kt_DME/y from 360 kt_CO2/y input with CAPEX of €85.7M baseline.
summary: Dimethyl ether synthesis from CO2 and hydrogen produces 186.7 kt_DME/y from 360 kt_CO2/y input. CAPEX baseline €85.7M (range €53.6–135.7M). MSP ranges 695–1060 €/t_product with cost per ton CO2 avoided of 543–1969 €/t_CO2eq,av. Life cycle GHG emissions are 77–96% lower than fossil counterpart (28.8 MJ/kg LHV, 2304 kg_CO2eq/t, fossil price 356 €/t). Geographic performance shows Chile has lowest production costs.

description: Long-term dimethyl ether synthesis with MSP 2.2–3.0 times higher than fossil counterpart and improved cost competitiveness through policy incentives.
summary: Long-term DME synthesis maintains MSP 695–1060 €/t_product (2.2–3.0 times fossil price). Cost per ton CO2 avoided improves to 225–537 €/t_CO2eq,av baseline range, estimated to fall below 230 €/t_CO2eq,av. Life cycle GHG emissions remain 77–96% lower than fossil counterpart. Economics align with existing EU climate change mitigation policies. Geographic performance shows Chile ~5% lower than Spain, 15% lower than Iceland, 45% lower than Netherlands.

description: Ammonia synthesis via Haber-Bosch process using hydrogen from renewable electrolysis and CO2 from low-temperature solid sorbent direct air capture.
tech_type: Haber-Bosch with DAC-sourced CO2 and renewable H2
summary: Haber-Bosch process converting CO2 and renewable hydrogen to ammonia. Plant operates 8000 h/year with 277.4 kt ammonia/year capacity based on 360 kt CO2/year input. Baseline capital cost €132.2M (range €107.9–€165.8M). Hydrogen production specific energy: AEC 55.1 kWh/kg, PEM 57.9 kWh/kg, SOEC 34.1 kWh/kg electric + 8.3 kWh/kg thermal. Investment lifetime 25 years with 1.5 debt-to-equity ratio. Life-cycle GHG emissions 72–96% lower than fossil-based ammonia (~107–740 kg CO2 eq/t depending on location and electrolyzer). Minimum selling price ~410–670 €/t long-term. Cost of CO2 avoided: 203–1087 €/t CO2 eq near-term.

description: Long-term projection (2050) of ammonia synthesis via Haber-Bosch with renewable hydrogen and CO2 capture, showing improved technology maturity and reduced costs.
tech_type: Haber-Bosch with DAC-sourced CO2 and renewable H2
summary: Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis in long-term future with full commercialization. Same 8000 h/year operation producing 277.4 kt/year. Electrolyzer capital costs significantly reduced: AEC €527.2/kW (range €306.5–€774.5), PEM €473.5/kW (range €257.9–€700.5), SOEC €958.3/kW (range €566.5–€1723.3). Improved hydrogen efficiency: AEC 48.9 kWh/kg (45.47–52.0), PEM 53.1 kWh/kg (47.0–64.0). Electrolyzer stack lifetimes: AEC 87,500 h, PEM 85,420 h, SOEC 71,991 h. Minimum selling price 410–670 €/t (54.2% reduction from 2035). Life-cycle GHG emissions 72–96% reduction vs fossil (74–740 kg CO2 eq/t). Cost of CO2 avoided: 110–266 €/t CO2 eq. Geothermal (Iceland): €25.6/MWh with 13.9 kg CO2 eq/MWh.

description: Standard Haber-Bosch process for ammonia synthesis from hydrogen and nitrogen extracted from air via air separation unit.
summary: Standard Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis with hydrogen from water electrolysis and nitrogen from air separation. Plant operates 8000 h/year (ramp-up: 30% year 1, 70% year 2) producing 277.4 kt ammonia/year. Baseline capital cost €132.2M (range €107.9–€165.8M). Investment lifetime 25 years with 1.5 debt-to-equity ratio. Location-dependent cost factors from Iceland baseline: Netherlands +29%, Spain +45%, Chile +17%. Long-term minimum selling price 410–670 €/t. Life-cycle GHG emissions 72–96% lower than fossil-based ammonia. Netherlands shows lowest emissions (~6% lower than Iceland, 50% lower than Spain, 55% lower than Chile). Cost of CO2 avoided near-term: 203–1087 €/t, long-term: 110–266 €/t.

description: Urea synthesis via conversion of ammonia and CO2, where ammonia derives from Haber-Bosch and CO2 from low-temperature direct air capture.
summary: Urea synthesis converting ammonia and CO2 to urea product. Plant operates 8000 h/year (ramp-up: 30% year 1, 70% year 2) with 491.8 kt/year capacity (highest among assessed products). Baseline capital cost €50.1M (range €24.6–€74.2M). Investment lifetime 25 years. Location-dependent cost variations from Iceland baseline: Netherlands +29%, Spain +45%, Chile +17%. Long-term minimum selling price 360–510 €/t with Chile lowest cost, most cost-competitive with fossil counterparts (<2.5x for most locations). Life-cycle GHG emissions 68–89% lower than fossil-based urea. Fossil benchmark: €202/t, 1406 kg CO2 eq/t (2020). Cost of CO2 avoided: near-term 203–1087 €/t, long-term 110–266 €/t (below 230 €/t aligns with EU climate policies). Discount rate 5–8%, scaling factor 0.6–0.9.

description: Thermally integrated process converting methanol to mixed olefins through optimized heat integration, compressors, and separation units.
summary: Methanol-to-olefins (MTO) conversion with thermal integration optimization. Plant operates 8000 h/year (ramp-up: 30% year 1, 70% year 2) producing 93.8 kt/year mixed olefins. Baseline capital cost €92.1M (range €77.0–€107.1M), includes compressors, heat exchangers, and separation units. Investment lifetime 25 years. Location-dependent advantages in long-term: Iceland baseline, Netherlands/Spain/Chile competitive. Long-term minimum selling price 1515–2240 €/t (among highest-cost products); Chile ~5% lower than Spain, 15% lower than Iceland, 45% lower than Netherlands. Life-cycle GHG emissions (cradle-to-grave) 50–87% lower than fossil olefins (benchmarked against EU PET plastic: 60% recycling, 20% incineration, 20% landfilling). Netherlands (offshore wind) shows lowest emissions due to electricity consumption significance. Cost of CO2 avoided: high variability near-term (€5062–26739/t CO2 eq), long-term 395–1730 €/t. SOEC sensitivity: Netherlands 42–218 €/t MSP reduction, Chile 3–11 €/t. Discount rate 5–8%, scaling factor 0.6–0.9.
